readings.title: The Insect Folk — A Large Family: Sorting the Straight-Wings
readings.challenge: Sort living things into groups by what they share, and test the groups against exceptions.
readings.focus: The class sorts the insects it has met into orders by looking at wings, mouths and legs.
readings.context: Margaret Warner Morley’s The Insect Folk (1903) is written as a teacher talking with a group of children (Nell, May, John, Ned, Mollie and others) while they look at real insects. Its science is more than a hundred years old. Scientists sort insects into large groups called orders, and many order names are built from Greek words: pteron means wing. This chapter reviews insects from earlier chapters: cockroaches (Croton bugs), the praying mantis, walking sticks, grasshoppers and crickets, dragon flies, May flies, stone flies and the silver fish. The edition prints “pteran” for “pteron” once near the end.

excerpt.locator: “A Large Family,” the whole chapter; opens “The crickets, grasshoppers, walking sticks, praying mantes, and cockroaches, strange as…”; closes “…from its bristle tail, _thysanos_, in Greek, meaning a tassel, and _oura_, the tail.”.

questions.prompt: What do all the Orthoptera share? Find two features.
facilitatorNotes: Under wings folded in long straight lines (which gives the name “straight-wing”), mouth parts made for biting, and young that look like the adults but without wings.
evidence: the under wings are folded down in long straight lines
The Orthoptera all have mouth parts made to bite with.

questions.prompt: John objects that walking sticks have no wings. How does the teacher answer, and is it a good answer?
facilitatorNotes: Their tropical relatives have wings, so they belong to a winged family. A group is defined by its relatives and shared features, not by every single member. Readers may find this convincing or want more evidence.
evidence: Not our walking sticks, but yet they belong to a winged family.

questions.prompt: How does the class name the four kinds of Orthoptera, and why does the teacher say grouping helps?
facilitatorNotes: By how they move or use their legs: running, grasping, walking and jumping. Grouping things that are alike makes them easier to remember. The children even argue over the best word, “grabbing” or “grasping.”
evidence: If we can group together things that are like each other, it is easier to remember them.
because grasping sounds a little better than grabbing

questions.prompt: Why does the dragon fly not belong in this family?
facilitatorNotes: Its wings are stiff and finely veined, all four alike, with no wing covers, and its young look nothing like the adults. So it has its own order, the Odonata.
evidence: all four of them are alike
But they certainly do not look like their parents!

readings.title: The Insect Folk — Water Bugs: Back-Swimmers, Giants and Mrs. Shore Bug
readings.challenge: Compare three insects that live by water, and separate facts from a mistaken idea.
readings.focus: Morley describes three water bugs and corrects a “foolish notion” with evidence.
readings.context: Margaret Warner Morley’s The Insect Folk (1903) is written as a teacher talking with a group of children (Nell, May, John, Ned, Mollie and others) while they look at real insects. Its science is more than a hundred years old. A keel is the ridge along the bottom of a boat. The tibia and femur are parts of an insect’s leg, like a shin and a thigh. Progeny means offspring. Morley uses “bug” for one order of insects with sucking beaks.
readings.contentNote: The giant water bug kills fish and other prey by sucking their blood, and the children are warned that some water bugs stab or bite.

excerpt.locator: “The Funny Back-Swimmers,” “The Giant Water Bug” and “Little Mrs. Shore Bug,” three whole short chapters; opens “What, John? You know a water boatman that swims on its back?”; closes “…her short flights, and so she will continue to do as long as you continue to chase her.”.

questions.prompt: How does the back-swimmer’s shape explain the way it swims?
facilitatorNotes: Unlike the flat water boatman, its back is shaped like a boat’s keel, so it turns over and swims on that keel, rowing with its long hind legs.
evidence: its back is not flat but is shaped like the keel of a boat
it just turns over and swims with its keel-shaped back in the water

questions.prompt: Some people thought giant water bugs did not exist before electric lights. Why did they think so, and why does Morley call it “a very foolish notion”?
facilitatorNotes: They first noticed the bugs lying dead under street lamps. But the bugs had lived for thousands of years; people had simply not seen them. Noticing something for the first time does not make it new.
evidence: they imagined they did not exist until electric lights were invented
the bugs were here thousands of years before electric lights were dreamed of

questions.prompt: What surprising job does the father giant water bug have in some species?
facilitatorNotes: The female lays the eggs on his back, and he carries them until they hatch. Morley’s word “obliged” jokes that he has no choice.
evidence: she puts them on the back of her mate
who is obliged to carry all of his progeny about with him

questions.prompt: How does Mrs. Shore Bug escape being caught, and why might Morley call her “Mrs.”?
facilitatorNotes: She flies a little way ahead, lands, and is gone again the moment you reach for her. Calling her “Mrs.” makes her a teasing character; readers may say it makes her memorable, though it is not science.
evidence: but when you think you have her, she isn't there!

readings.title: The Insect Folk — A Queer Fellow: Legs or Feelers?
readings.challenge: Follow an argument between two observers and find the evidence that settles it.
readings.focus: The children argue about what they see, and the insect answers by moving.
readings.context: Margaret Warner Morley’s The Insect Folk (1903) is written as a teacher talking with a group of children (Nell, May, John, Ned, Mollie and others) while they look at real insects. Its science is more than a hundred years old. The insect in the box is a thread-legged bug, though the chapter does not name it. Antennae are an insect’s feelers; a mantis catches prey with folding front legs. Count the guesses the children make before the answer comes.

excerpt.locator: “A Queer Fellow,” the whole chapter; opens “What do you suppose is in this box?”; closes “…never been stung by one. We often see them walking about in the grass and along paths.”.

questions.prompt: Ned and Mollie disagree about the two front threads. What evidence does each give?
facilitatorNotes: Ned sees joints like the other legs and says they are legs; Mollie sees no little feet and says they are antennae. Each points to a real detail.
evidence: Ned says those front ones look to him to be jointed just like the others
Mollie says they have no little feet like the others

questions.prompt: What finally settles the question?
facilitatorNotes: The insect moves: what looked like its head separates into two folded front legs, so the threads in front are antennae after all. Watching the living insect settles what arguing could not.
evidence: that long part in front is not its head!
So the long threads are antennae after all.

questions.prompt: What do the children guess the creature is, and why is “a--bug!” a surprise?
facilitatorNotes: A walking stick, “Mr. Walking Threads,” a mantis. Its wings rule out a walking stick. It turns out to belong to the same order as the big, flat giant water bug, though it is thin as thread.
evidence: But we know you are not a walking stick because our walking sticks have no wings.
this little threadlike creature belongs to the same order as the big flat giant water bug

readings.title: The Insect Folk — A Bad Bug: Everything but Wings and Good Manners
readings.challenge: Notice when a writer’s jokes become claims, and test whether the claims hold up.
readings.focus: Morley makes the bed bug both a joke and a warning.
readings.context: Margaret Warner Morley’s The Insect Folk (1903) is written as a teacher talking with a group of children (Nell, May, John, Ned, Mollie and others) while they look at real insects. Its science is more than a hundred years old. This chapter is about the bed bug. Rudimentary means small and undeveloped; spiracles are an insect’s breathing holes; to sally forth is to rush out; voracious means very hungry; emaciated means very thin; vigilance is watchfulness.
readings.contentNote: Morley’s idea that the bed bug lost its wings because it “preferred” hiding in cracks is not how scientists now explain such changes.

excerpt.locator: “A Bad Bug,” the whole chapter; opens “Now, here is a bug we all loathe. It is round and flat, and reddish brown in color, and…”; closes “…bugs, only they have wings, and live on flowers or in the cracks of the bark of trees.”.

questions.prompt: Find two places where Morley jokes about the bed bug. What attitude do the jokes show?
facilitatorNotes: It has everything a bug should have “but wings and good manners”; its young are “ghosts of bugs,” but very hungry ones. She treats it as a villain the reader can laugh at.
evidence: it has everything a bug should have but wings and good manners
They look like ghosts of bugs

questions.prompt: Morley says the bug lost its wings because it “preferred” hiding in cracks, “which served it right.” Which part is observed, and which part is a story?
facilitatorNotes: The small scales where wings should be can be seen. The reason she gives treats the insect as choosing and being punished, which no one could observe; scientists today explain such changes differently.
evidence: these scales are rudimentary wings
It once had wings, but it preferred to go slipping about in cracks

questions.prompt: Why can even one bed bug become a problem in a house?
facilitatorNotes: They hide in cracks, can live a very long time without food, and breed so fast that one can infest a house within weeks.
evidence: they can live a very long time with nothing to eat
may cause it to become generally infested in a few weeks

readings.title: The Insect Folk — The Well Protected Stink Bug: Smells as Messages
readings.challenge: Follow an explanation that widens from one insect to a general idea.
readings.focus: A bad smell can be a defence, and a sweet one can be a message.
readings.context: Margaret Warner Morley’s The Insect Folk (1903) is written as a teacher talking with a group of children (Nell, May, John, Ned, Mollie and others) while they look at real insects. Its science is more than a hundred years old. The thorax is the middle part of an insect’s body; to eject is to squirt out; to repel is to drive away. Mercaptan is a chemical with a very strong smell, and a grain is a tiny old unit of weight.

excerpt.locator: “The Well Protected Stink Bug,” the whole chapter; opens “One of the bugs we know the best and like the least is the stink bug.”; closes “…them, however, eat fruits and vegetables, and some species do a vast amount of mischief.”.

questions.prompt: When does the stink bug make its smell, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Only when it is disturbed or startled, as when berry-pickers jostle the bushes. The smell drives off enemies, and very few birds will touch a stink bug.
evidence: If the stink bug is not disturbed, it does not give forth the bad odor
They wish to repel their enemies.

questions.prompt: How are pleasant insect smells used differently from bad ones?
facilitatorNotes: Bad smells drive enemies away; pleasant ones attract, for example by leading a mate from far off. Morley calls this “one way of talking.”
evidence: The pleasant odors are not used to repel, but to attract.
this pleasant odor is one way of talking

questions.prompt: Why does Morley bring in the human nose and mercaptan?
facilitatorNotes: If even our nose can detect an unbelievably tiny amount, insects with much keener smell could be strongly affected by odours we never notice. She argues from a comparison.
evidence: Insects can detect odors much better than we can.
insects that can smell very, very much better than we would be greatly influenced by the odors of other insects

readings.title: The Insect Folk — Leaf Hoppers and Tree Hoppers: A Contested Warfare
readings.challenge: Weigh a writer’s delight in insects against her account of fighting them.
readings.focus: Pretty insects can be pests, and people fight them with sprays and poisons.
readings.context: Margaret Warner Morley’s The Insect Folk (1903) is written as a teacher talking with a group of children (Nell, May, John, Ned, Mollie and others) while they look at real insects. Its science is more than a hundred years old. To moult is to shed an old skin. Kerosene emulsion, Paris green and blue vitriol were sprays used in 1903; Paris green contains arsenic and is no longer used on crops. Brownies were little elf characters in popular picture books of the time.
readings.contentNote: The chapter describes spraying plants with poisons, some now known to be dangerous and no longer used.

excerpt.locator: “Pretty Leaf Hoppers” and “The Comical Tree Hoppers,” two whole chapters; opens “Just see this bush! Be careful not to shake it.”; closes “…They seldom come in swarms like some of the leaf hoppers, though sometimes they do.”.

questions.prompt: What sound do the leaf hoppers make when May bumps the bush, and what does the comparison tell you?
facilitatorNotes: Like raindrops pattering on the leaves: a great many tiny insects jumping at once.
evidence: they do sound like rain drops pattering on the leaves

questions.prompt: Morley calls the struggle between farmers and insects “a closely contested warfare.” What does each side do?
facilitatorNotes: People plough, plant and weed; the insects find a feast; people spray poisons, burn eggs and study the insects’ habits. Her joke that the insects feel “very happy, no doubt” lets the reader see the war from their side too.
evidence: it is a closely contested warfare all the time
feeling very happy, no doubt, to have found such a feast

questions.prompt: Morley calls the poisoned vines “very gaudy.” Does she seem worried by the poisons? What might a reader today add?
facilitatorNotes: She says they are “very poisonous” but describes the bright colour lightly. Today we know such poisons can harm people, animals and helpful insects, which is why some are banned. She still insists that insects are “so very interesting.”
evidence: Paris green and blue vitriol, both very poisonous
Although insects are so very interesting, we have to protect ourselves against many species in order to live.

questions.prompt: Why are the tree hoppers “comical,” and why are they seldom a nuisance?
facilitatorNotes: They are hard and three-cornered with humps or horns, like “animated beechnuts” or Brownies; they rarely come in swarms large enough to do damage.
evidence: like animated beechnuts, as somebody has said
there are not usually enough of them to do damage

readings.title: The Insect Folk — Fairy Lacewing: The Aphis Lion
readings.challenge: Hold two very different pictures of the same insect at once.
readings.focus: A delicate green “fairy” has a ferocious young, and the mother protects her eggs in a clever way.
readings.context: Margaret Warner Morley’s The Insect Folk (1903) is written as a teacher talking with a group of children (Nell, May, John, Ned, Mollie and others) while they look at real insects. Its science is more than a hundred years old. The corydalus, or dobson, is a large insect from the chapter before. Neuroptera means “nerve-winged.” Aphids, also called plant lice, suck the juices of plants. A cannibal here is an animal that eats its own kind; metamorphosis is the change from young to adult; a pupa is the resting stage between. Morley says the adult lacewing does not eat; in fact many kinds feed on nectar, pollen or small insects.

excerpt.locator: “Fairy Lacewing,” the whole chapter; opens “Here is our little Lacewing.”; closes “…us get rid of the aphids, and we should never kill a lacewing or a child of the lacewing.”.

questions.prompt: Which words make the adult lacewing seem like a fairy? What surprise does it hold?
facilitatorNotes: She is “a woodland fairy clad all in green” with golden eyes and lacy wings. But touch her and she gives off a nasty smell, her one strong defence.
evidence: like a woodland fairy clad all in green
It gives forth such an offensive odor

questions.prompt: Why is the lacewing’s larva called the aphis lion?
facilitatorNotes: It has tremendous jaws and runs about “like a ravening lion,” devouring aphids and any insect it can overpower.
evidence: It is also called the aphis lion.
runs about like a ravening lion seeking some living thing to devour

questions.prompt: How does the mother lacewing keep her young from eating each other?
facilitatorNotes: She lays each egg on top of a stiff silk stalk, like a little forest. A larva that hatches drops to the leaf and never discovers the unhatched eggs above its head.
evidence: each one is on top of a slender stalk
like a little forest, with an egg for each tree top

questions.prompt: Morley says we should never kill a lacewing. What is her reason, and is it the only good reason to protect an insect?
facilitatorNotes: It eats the aphids that damage plants, so it is “our very good friend.” Her reason is usefulness to people; readers may add others, such as beauty or the wish to understand it.
evidence: You see the aphis lion is our very good friend.
we should never kill a lacewing or a child of the lacewing

readings.title: The Insect Folk — The Ant Lion: A Trap in the Sand
readings.challenge: Follow an investigation step by step: watch, dig, then watch again.
readings.focus: The children find out what hides at the bottom of a sand funnel, and how its trap works.
readings.context: Margaret Warner Morley’s The Insect Folk (1903) is written as a teacher talking with a group of children (Nell, May, John, Ned, Mollie and others) while they look at real insects. Its science is more than a hundred years old. A funnel here is a cone-shaped pit; a trowel is a small hand shovel; a cocoon is a case spun before the resting stage. Nymphs are the young of insects such as grasshoppers, which grow into adults without a resting stage.
readings.contentNote: The ant lion seizes ants and drags them underground to eat them.

excerpt.locator: “The Ant Lion,” the whole chapter; opens “John has found something he wants us all to see.”; closes “Young grasshoppers are sometimes called nymphs instead of larvae.”.

questions.prompt: What do the children see happen at the funnel before they know what lives there?
facilitatorNotes: An ant slides down the smooth sides, two curved jaws leap out, and the ant is dragged out of sight. They see the result first and then ask who did it.
evidence: from the bottom of the funnel leap out two curved jaws
Who can be living down there at the bottom of the funnel?

questions.prompt: How does the ant lion dig its trap, and what does it do when an ant tries to climb out?
facilitatorNotes: It shovels the sand away using its own head as a trowel, and it flings sand at a climbing ant until the ant slips back down.
evidence: it is shovelling the sand away with its head
the ant lion down below is flinging sand at it

questions.prompt: Morley says the change into a pupa happens in this order and “In no other order that we have studied.” Why do those last words matter?
facilitatorNotes: They limit the claim to the insects in this book so far. Other insects, such as the caddis flies in the next chapter, also rest as pupae, so the statement is not true of all insects.
evidence: In no other order that we have studied
